q: Who is the author of the lesson "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi"?
o: Madhu Kankaria
Mannu Bhandari
Mahadevi Verma
Krishna Sobti
e: The author of "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi" is the noted Hindi writer Madhu Kankaria.

q: To which literary genre does "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi" belong?
o: One-act play
Mythological epic
Biography
Travelogue
e: It is a travelogue in which the author vividly narrates her journey through Sikkim and the Himalayas.

q: From whom did the author learn the prayer "Sana-sana haath jodi"?
o: A Buddhist monk
Her friend Mani
A Nepali young woman
Jiten Narge’s grandmother
e: The author learned this prayer from a young Nepali woman during her trip.

q: What is the meaning of the prayer "Sana-sana haath jodi"?
o: May my journey finish without obstacles
Joining my tiny hands, I pray that my whole life be dedicated to goodness
O God, grant me immense wealth and splendor
May snow always stay on the mountains
e: This Nepali prayer means: "Joining my little hands, I pray that my entire life be dedicated to goodness."

q: Which city did the author call the "City of Hardworking Kings"?
o: Gangtok (Gantok)
Yumthang
Katao
Darjeeling
e: Seeing the hardworking people of Sikkim’s capital Gangtok, the author called it the "City of Hardworking Kings".

q: What was the name of the author’s guide-cum-driver in "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi"?
o: Tenzing Norgay
Kanchan Lama
Dorje Bhutia
Jiten Narge
e: Jiten Narge was the author’s knowledgeable Nepali guide-cum-driver who introduced her to Sikkim’s places and culture.

q: How far is Yumthang from Gangtok as mentioned in the chapter?
o: 250 kilometers
50 kilometers
149 kilometers
80 kilometers
e: Jiten Narge informed the author that Yumthang lies 149 kilometers away from Gangtok.

q: In Buddhism, how many white prayer flags are hoisted when someone passes away?
o: 1008 white flags
108 white flags
51 white flags
21 white flags
e: On the death of a Buddhist, 108 white flags are hoisted at a sacred spot outside the town for the peace of the soul.

q: What kind of prayer flags are hoisted in Sikkim at the start of an auspicious new venture?
o: Colorful flags
Only black flags
Only white flags
Yellow metal plates
e: White flags mark mourning, whereas colorful flags are hoisted when starting a new auspicious work.

q: Kabi Longstok is mentioned in the lesson for the shooting of which famous film?
o: Sangam
Sholay
Mother India
Guide
e: Pointing out Kabi Longstok, Jiten told the author that the film "Guide" was shot there.

q: Which major river’s valley and rushing waters are repeatedly described in "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi"?
o: Godavari River
Son River
Teesta River
Yamuna River
e: Throughout the travelogue, the beauty and rushing flow of the Teesta River accompany the journey.

q: Which famous waterfall is seen on the route to Yumthang in "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi"?
o: Dhuandhar Falls
Seven Sisters Waterfall
Jog Falls
Hundru Falls
e: On the road from Gangtok to Yumthang, the travelers see the stunning Seven Sisters Waterfall.

q: Which place is referred to as the "Switzerland of India" in the lesson?
o: Katao
Gangtok
Patna
Shimla
e: Because of its snowy valleys and untouched natural beauty, Katao is called the "Switzerland of India".

q: What did the author’s friend Mani say after seeing the snow at Katao?
o: It is too hot here
Coming here was a waste of time
This place is very dirty
It is even more beautiful than Switzerland
e: Mani, who had visited Switzerland, exclaimed that Katao was even more beautiful than Switzerland.

q: What did Jiten explain about spinning the prayer wheel (Dharmachakra) inside a cottage in Sikkim?
o: Spinning it brings instant rain
Spinning it showers money
Spinning it washes away all sins
Spinning it generates electricity
e: Jiten explained that it is a Dharmachakra (prayer wheel), believed to wash away all sins when spun.

q: How did the Sikkimese girl selling chips in Yumthang reply when asked if she was from Sikkim?
o: I am a foreign tourist
I am Indian
I am only Nepali
I am Tibetan
e: The girl proudly replied, "No, I am Indian," filling the author with deep joy about national integration.

q: What is "Khedum" described as in the chapter?
o: The abode of gods and goddesses, where anyone who litters is believed to die
A large modern shopping mall
A military armory
The capital of Nepal
e: Jiten explained that Khedum is a sacred one-kilometer zone believed to be the abode of deities where no one litters.

q: With what tools were the mountain women breaking stones in Sikkim?
o: Large crane machines
Bulldozers
Wooden sticks
Spades and hammers
e: With their babies tied in baskets (doko) on their backs, the mountain women broke stones using spades and hammers.

q: Who is the author of the essay "Main Kyon Likhta Hoon?"?
o: Hazariprasad Dwivedi
Ramvriksh Benipuri
S.H. Vatsyayan "Ajneya"
Shivpoojan Sahay
e: The essay "Main Kyon Likhta Hoon?" is written by renowned Hindi writer S.H. Vatsyayan "Ajneya".

q: Which prose genre is "Main Kyon Likhta Hoon?"?
o: Collection of folk songs
Reflective essay
Historical play
Love story
e: It is a reflective, introspective essay in which the writer examines his own creative process.

q: According to Ajneya, what is the primary and truest reason a writer writes?
o: Inner compulsion (the urge to express and free oneself from inner experience)
Only greed for money
Winning government awards
Imitating others
e: Ajneya explains that a writer writes to recognize and gain release from an inner compulsion.

q: After visiting which country did Ajneya write the poem "Hiroshima"?
o: Germany
Russia
France
Japan
e: After visiting Hiroshima during his trip to Japan, Ajneya returned to India and wrote the poem "Hiroshima".

q: Which academic subject had Ajneya studied as a student?
o: Law
Medicine
Science
Commerce
e: The author mentions in the essay that he had been a science student and knew theoretically about radioactivity.

q: While walking down a street in Hiroshima, what did Ajneya see on a scorched stone?
o: A bouquet of fresh flowers
A long bright shadow (the silhouette of a human figure)
A gold coin
A war tank wheel
e: Seeing a pale silhouette imprinted on a scorched stone gave Ajneya a visceral realization of a person vaporized by the atomic blast.

q: Where was Ajneya sitting when he actually wrote the poem "Hiroshima"?
o: While sitting in a train in India
Inside a Hiroshima hospital
In a Japanese hotel room
Inside an airplane
e: After returning to India, one day while sitting on a train, the poem "Hiroshima" suddenly poured forth.

q: According to Ajneya, which of the following can serve as external pressures for writing?
o: Atomic explosions and earthquakes
Forest travel and mountain winds
Sleep and laziness
Editors’ requests, publishers’ reminders, and financial need
e: Editors’ requests, publishers’ insistence, and financial necessity act as external prompts, though inner compulsion remains primary.

q: What did Ajneya see in the hospital at Hiroshima?
o: A conference of doctors
Healthy children playing
People suffering for years from radiation injuries
Only new modern machines
e: At the hospital, he saw victims suffering for years from radiation, though at that stage it remained merely an external "experience".

q: What does Ajneya describe as deeper and more decisive for writing than mere "experience" (anubhav)?
o: Friendship with famous people
Anubhuti (deep inner realization born of sensibility and imagination)
Knowledge of grammar
Printing technology
e: Ajneya distinguishes anubhav (what happens before us) from anubhuti (what penetrates deeply via sensibility and imagination to spark creation).

q: The tragedy observed by Ajneya in Hiroshima was the result of which event?
o: Atomic bomb explosion
Volcanic eruption
Massive ocean tsunami
Earthquake and landslide
e: Ajneya witnessed the aftermath of the atomic bomb explosion and radiation devastation in Hiroshima.

q: According to Ajneya, without what is genuine creative writing impossible?
o: Without an expensive library
Without foreign travel
Without newspaper advertisements
Without inner realization (anubhuti) and inner compulsion
e: External pressures are secondary; true creative work arises only when inner realization compels expression.

q: How did the city of Gangtok appear to the author at night?
o: Like a ship sinking in the sea
Like a dark, silent forest
As if the sky had turned upside down and all the stars were scattered twinkling below
Completely invisible in thick fog
e: Looking at the lights glittering on the mountain slopes, she felt as if the starry sky lay inverted upon the earth.

q: What legend is associated with the stone bearing Guru Nanak Dev’s footprints near Gangtok?
o: He won a battle there
It is said rice spilled from Guru Nanak’s plate there, and rice grows wherever those grains fell
He built a golden temple there
The Ganga originated from there
e: Jiten recounted the belief that rice spilled from Guru Nanak’s plate onto the ground, blessing those spots with rice cultivation.

q: What special custom is followed regarding the Buddhist prayer flags in Sikkim?
o: These flags are never taken down; they wear away naturally on their own
They are taken down and washed every evening
They are hoisted only one day a week
They are chained with iron
e: Inscribed with prayers, these flags are never removed manually and are left to fade naturally in the mountain wind.

q: What benefit has come from Katao not being turned into a commercial tourist spot?
o: No ticket is required there
Many huge hotels have opened there
Only summer weather prevails there
Its natural beauty, cleanliness, and fresh snow have remained preserved
e: Jiten explained that precisely because Katao lacked commercial shops and tourist crowds, its pristine snow and beauty survived.

q: How was the life of hill children in Layung different from that of children in the plains?
o: There were no schools there
They only rowed boats
After school, they helped their mothers, grazed cattle, fetched water, and carried bundles of firewood
They played video games all day
e: Mountain life is arduous; children walked several kilometers up steep slopes to school and helped their families with chores afterward.

q: What profound thought struck the author upon seeing hill women breaking stones with babies strapped to their backs?
o: "These women should move to cities for trade"
"How little they take in return, yet how much they give back to society"
"Building roads in the hills is useless"
"These women are very wealthy"
e: Seeing their grueling labor, the author realized how these humble workers give back immensely to society while receiving so little.

q: What did the Indian soldiers guarding the freezing Sikkim border say to the author?
o: "We stand guard here in this bitter cold so that you can sleep peacefully"
"Photography is strictly banned, leave immediately"
"We get very high salaries here"
"We are troubled by the heat"
e: Guarding the border in sub-zero cold, a soldier smiled and said they stood watch so citizens back home could sleep in peace.

q: What unusual fact did the author’s companion Mani share about mountain dogs?
o: That mountain dogs never sleep
That mountain dogs eat only snow
That they guide tourists on trails
That mountain dogs bark only on moonlit nights
e: Mani told the author that these mountain dogs stay quiet otherwise and bark only on moonlit nights.

q: What kind of atmosphere did the author experience by the Teesta River in Layung during the evening?
o: Echoing with speeding trains
Filled with factory smoke
Deeply tranquil, still, and filled with spiritual calm in nature’s lap
A noisy crowded marketplace
e: Outside the small wooden house, the gentle murmur of the Teesta and nocturnal stillness gave the author profound peace.

q: What reason did Jiten give for the lack of snow in Yumthang itself?
o: Drying up of the river
Rising pollution and global warming (climate warming)
Snow season having not started yet
Proximity to the sea
e: They learned that rising pollution had reduced snowfall in Yumthang, forcing tourists to climb higher to Katao for snow.

q: What was the road leading up to Katao like?
o: Extremely narrow, perilous, icy, and shrouded in mist
A straight six-lane paved highway
A flat desert track
A brightly lit wide bridge
e: The mountain track to Katao was treacherous, narrow, icy, and mist-covered, making driving very risky.

q: What danger faced by road-construction workers in the mountains is mentioned in the chapter?
o: Attacks by wild lions
Ocean hurricanes
Market recession
Risk of fatal falls on narrow cliffs or accidents during dynamite blasting
e: Widening impossible mountain roads with dynamite and working on sheer cliffs often cost laborers their lives.

q: How did the author describe the rapidly changing landscapes and moods of nature during her mountain ascent?
o: Like city buildings changing paint
Like pages of a book tearing
Like an enchanting play of illusion and shadow—sunshine, clouds, and mist shifting constantly
Like everything was static and monotonous stone
e: Watching clouds, waterfalls, sunlight, and mist shift moment by moment, she describes it as a magical play of light and shadow.

q: What did the author learn about Gangtok’s name "Gantok" and its topography?
o: It was named after a foreign king
"Gantok" means "hill/mountain" and the town is perched atop hills
"Gantok" means "seashore"
The city sits on completely flat plains
e: The text notes that "Gantok" means hill/mountain, and beyond it the Himalayas reveal their grandest scale.

q: What absence at Katao struck the author as a blessing, and why did tourists look for boots?
o: There were no shops or rented snow boots for knee-deep snow, yet that absence kept Katao unspoiled
There were no mountains there
The river water was boiling hot
Only Hindi movies were playing there
e: Although the author lacked snow boots because there were no rental shops, she admired how lack of commercialization kept Katao pristine.

q: How does the author connect the sacred feeling of Himalayan rivers and prayer wheels with the rest of India?
o: Sikkim’s culture is hostile to India
Rivers flow only in Sikkim
People have forgotten to revere rivers
In beliefs about purity, washing away sins, and reverence for nature, the soul of all India feels united
e: Seeing the prayer wheel, she reflects that across all of India, people share a common spiritual thread of faith and reverence.

q: Why did the author consider Jiten Narge an exemplary tour guide?
o: Because he took them only to luxury hotels
Because he stayed completely silent
Because he sensitively shared accurate insights into local culture, geography, folklore, and people’s lives
Because he only sang songs
e: Jiten was attentive, well-informed, and empathetic, explaining local legends, ecology, and hardships along every mile.

q: What kind of messages were written on the roadside signboards along the treacherous mountain routes?
o: "Seashore ahead"
Warnings like "Drive slowly, children wait at home" and "Better late than an accident"
"Drive at maximum speed here"
"Littering is mandatory here"
e: Border Roads signboards warned drivers with reminders about family waiting at home and caution against speeding.

q: Why does Ajneya consider answering "Why do I write?" difficult?
o: Because though it looks simple, its true answer lies in the deep inner layers of a writer’s life
Because the author does not know how to write
Because nobody ever asked this question
Because paper and pens are expensive
e: Ajneya notes that this seemingly simple question cannot be answered briefly because it touches deep psychological layers.

q: According to Ajneya, what does a writer seek liberation from by writing?
o: From family responsibilities
From legal lawsuits
From rules of grammar
From his inner compulsion, in order to view and understand it objectively from outside
e: When an intense feeling churns inside, writing externalizes it so the writer can observe it objectively and gain release.

q: Why does Ajneya give the example of a lazy person waking up late despite the alarm?
o: To prove all writers are lazy
To explain Japanese train schedules
To illustrate how external nudges (like an alarm) can prompt action, just as publishers’ requests aid writing—even if the urge is internal
To argue that waking early is harmful
e: Just as an alarm assists a sleeper’s own wish to wake up, external deadlines assist an existing creative urge.

q: Why could Ajneya not immediately write a poem even after seeing radiation victims in the Hiroshima hospital?
o: Because he did not know Japanese
Because until then it remained only an external "experience", not yet a deeply felt inner "anubhuti"
Because he lacked a pen and diary
Because writing was banned in the hospital
e: He explains that the hospital visit was only an external observation; inner realization struck later when he saw the human shadow on stone.

q: What happened in Ajneya’s mind the moment he saw the bright human shadow etched on the stone?
o: He envisioned a person standing there who was vaporized in an instant by the nuclear flash, leaving only a shadow burned onto the stone
He thought a street artist painted it for fun
He thought a tall tree cast that shadow
He thought it was a movie poster
e: Seeing the shadow hit him like a sudden slap—the full horror of the nuclear flash crystallized before his sensibility.

q: Which two faculties does Ajneya credit for transforming external experience into deep inner realization (anubhuti)?
o: Wealth and status
Logic and mathematics
Anger and revenge
Sensibility (samvedana) and imagination (kalpana)
e: According to Ajneya, when raw experience is internalized through sensibility and imagination, it becomes anubhuti.

q: Why does Ajneya mention that he already had factual knowledge about radioactivity before visiting Hiroshima?
o: To discourage writers from studying science
To remind readers of Hiroshima’s date
To show that mere bookish or scientific knowledge cannot produce creative art until it becomes felt inner realization
To boast about his science degree
e: Although he knew nuclear physics theoretically, only the visceral encounter with the stone shadow turned fact into poetic truth.

q: How did Ajneya view his poem "Hiroshima" after writing it on the train?
o: He wept over its grammar
Regardless of whether critics judged it good or bad, he felt fulfilled because it was born of genuine inner realization
He felt it should be burned immediately
He thought it would win a Nobel Prize
e: Ajneya says he did not care about external literary judgment; what mattered was that the poem sprang from authentic inner experience.

q: According to Ajneya, when does the true urge to write awaken within a writer?
o: When sensibility is so deeply stirred by an event that something within grows restless for expression
When a holiday falls on a festival
When a friend forces a pen into one’s hand
When exams are near
e: That inner restlessness which refuses to settle until expressed in words is the true source of writing.

q: What does Ajneya mean by "inner compulsion" (bhitari vivashata) in "Main Kyon Likhta Hoon?"?
o: A court’s legal order
Forced labor due to poverty
Weakness from physical illness
The internal pressure of felt experience demanding artistic expression
e: Inner compulsion is not an outside coercion, but the creative restlessness of a sensitive mind seeking expression.

q: According to Ajneya, why can no two writers give the exact same answer to "Why do I write?"?
o: Because no writer tells the truth
Because grammar rules keep changing
Because each writer’s inner temperament, life context, and sensibility are unique
Because all writers live in different countries
e: Since the creative process is deeply personal and internal, every writer discovers their own answer from within.

q: Between "inner compulsion" and "external pressure", which does Ajneya regard as enduring and essential?
o: Only editors’ requests
Inner compulsion
External pressure
Only financial greed
e: External pressure may act as a temporary catalyst, but enduring literature always stems from inner compulsion.

q: Passage: The author recalls the Nepali prayer while gazing at starlit Gangtok. What state of mind does this reflect?
o: Nature’s beauty elevating her mind above selfishness into a prayer for universal goodness
Worrying about travel expenses
Fear of getting lost
Hatred of urban crowds
e: Gangtok’s mesmerizing night view awakens a noble desire to dedicate life to goodness rather than selfish wishes.

q: Passage: "Delicate mountain women swinging spades and hammers, with babies tied in baskets on their backs." — What inner conflict did this arouse in the author?
o: A desire to buy pretty clothes
A plan to build houses in the hills
Anger toward driver Jiten
The stark contrast between the Himalayas’ sublime beauty and the harsh suffering of working mothers
e: Beside breathtaking scenery for tourists lay the grueling struggle of mothers laboring for survival, deeply shaking the author.

q: Seeing Layung children graze cattle and fetch water after school reveals what reality of mountain life?
o: Parents dislike their children
The government banned games
In harsh mountain terrain, survival demands collective labor from every family member, including children
The children refuse to study
e: Life in steep mountain regions is so demanding that even childhood involves sharing essential household chores.

q: Passage: Spinning the prayer wheel made the author feel that despite scientific progress, India’s soul is one. Why?
o: Because everyone lives in Gangtok
Because from the plains to the high Himalayas, people share similar spiritual beliefs, faith, and ideas of sin and merit
Because identical wheels are manufactured nationwide
Because science has eliminated religion
e: In the Buddhist prayer wheel, she recognized the same deep-rooted faith found across India’s varied traditions.

q: Passage: "The absence of any shops at Katao is a blessing for it." — Which environmental concern is hinted at here?
o: Unchecked commercial tourism brings litter, pollution, and destruction of fragile mountain ecosystems
Shopkeepers charge too much
Shops make tourists lose their way
Shops collapse in snow
e: Commercial crowding degrades fragile landscapes; Katao’s lack of shops protected its snow and pristine ecology.

q: What ecological function does the traditional belief about "Khedum" (where littering brings divine wrath) serve?
o: A business of selling idols
A trick to scare tourists away
Permission to cut forests
A folk consciousness using faith to keep sacred natural zones clean and pollution-free
e: Traditional beliefs often safeguard ecology; reverence for Khedum prevents people from polluting that pristine valley.

q: Whose narrow mindset is challenged by the Sikkimese girl’s proud reply, "I am Indian"?
o: Mountain dogs and yaks
Border soldiers
Those who mistakenly view residents of border and northeastern states as separate or outsiders
Foreign tourists
e: Mainlanders sometimes treat border residents as distant; her proud assertion affirms shared Indian identity.

q: Seeing soldiers braving sub-zero cold at the border, what realization dawned on the author about herself and citizens?
o: That heaters are enough for warmth
That civilians sleep comfortably and enjoy vacations only because soldiers risk their lives in harsh extremes
That soldiers should also go sightseeing
That war continues permanently on the border
e: The author is filled with gratitude and patriotism, realizing civilians’ comfort rests on soldiers’ silent sacrifice.

q: Passage: "So much was unfolding in the universe at once—cascading waterfalls, rushing Teesta below, drifting clouds above." — What philosophical feeling does this evoke?
o: Dissolution of the small human ego before cosmic vastness and a sense of oneness with flowing nature
Pride of human conquest over nature
Regret over wasted time
Greed for material possessions
e: Facing the grand, ceaseless motion of the Himalayas, the author feels her petty ego dissolve into serene cosmic unity.

q: Sitting by the Seven Sisters Waterfall, why did the author feel like an enchanted princess or ancient being?
o: Because she wore a princess costume
Because Jiten told a fairy tale
Because there was a power outage
The unearthly stillness and music of the waterfall transported her far beyond modern urban stress into a timeless realm
e: The waterfall’s pure music washed away her worldly worries and immersed her in primordial serenity.

q: What social inequality did the author reflect on while watching the stone-breaking women?
o: Rich people never travel to mountains
No roads are built in hills
Workers toil in hardship to build roads, while affluent travelers effortlessly enjoy scenic rides on those very roads
Only men visit the mountains
e: This social empathy highlights a stark irony: those whose sweat builds infrastructure receive the smallest share of comfort.

q: What philosophy of Buddhist society is reflected in the distinction between white and colorful prayer flags?
o: Treating colors as irreligious
Accepting death peacefully as a serene passage (white) while celebrating auspicious new beginnings (colorful)
Wailing loudly at death
Disliking the color white
e: In both mourning and celebration, prayer flags fluttering in the wind symbolize spreading peace, nonviolence, and goodwill.

q: Passage: "Because of rising pollution, snowfall has decreased." — What message does this episode give to the reader?
o: Human industrialization and pollution directly harm Himalayan glaciers and mountain climate
Lack of snow in mountains is beneficial
Pollution stays confined to cities
Tourists should carry more plastic
e: The missing snow in Yumthang serves as an urgent warning about climate change and ecological responsibility.

q: Throughout the journey, how did the contrast between Jiten’s cheerful narration and the harsh terrain affect the author?
o: It showed hill people are always gloomy
It showed vehicles cannot run in hills
It showed tourists are fearless
It showed how mountain folk remain cheerful, hospitable, and resilient despite harsh terrain and constant hazards
e: Despite rugged mountain hardships, the warmth and resilience of Jiten and local villagers made the journey unforgettable.

q: Context: The author marveled at nature’s marvelous arrangement of water, snow, and seasons in the Himalayas. What ecological balance did she admire?
o: Rivers never reaching the sea
Total absence of rain
Storing water as snow in winter and melting in summer to nourish thirsty plains via mighty rivers
Accumulating only bare rocks on peaks
e: She sees the snow peaks as nature’s water towers, storing winter snow to sustain rivers and life across the plains in summer.

q: How are working hill children portrayed in "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi"?
o: Dropping out to flee to cities
Helping mothers with water, firewood, and cattle after grueling school treks, showing both hardship and grit
Operating factory machinery
Begging from tourists
e: Unlike carefree plains children, mountain children balance steep treks to school with heavy domestic labor.

q: What perspective does the author’s traveling companion Mani represent in the travelogue?
o: An enthusiastic, well-traveled companion who recognizes the Indian Himalayas as surpassing even Switzerland
A cynical fault-finder
A coward wanting to turn back
Someone worried only about food
e: Mani’s lively enthusiasm and global comparison help underscore Katao’s extraordinary beauty.

q: How does the trip in "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi" transform from mere sightseeing into an "inner journey"?
o: Because she slept inside a cave
Because she spoke to nobody
Because she only read maps
Because alongside scenic beauty, she reflects deeply on laborers’ hardships, soldiers’ sacrifice, pollution, and inner purification
e: True travel expands the soul; Madhu Kankaria emerges with deeper social empathy, ecological awareness, and inner calm.

q: Passage: "Direct experience becomes anubhuti when internalized through sensibility and imagination." — Based on this, how did the hospital differ from the stone shadow?
o: The hospital had few people while the street was crowded
There was no difference between the two
The hospital was external experience, whereas the stone shadow jolted imagination and sensibility into deep anubhuti
The hospital was fake and the stone was real
e: Seeing suffering in the hospital stayed external, whereas the stone silhouette made the atomic tragedy come alive inwardly.

q: If a writer writes solely for a publisher’s money or editor’s pressure without inner realization, how would Ajneya view such writing?
o: It would require studying science
It would lack genuine creative depth and vitality because true inner compulsion is absent
It would become the world’s finest masterpiece
It would automatically match the poem "Hiroshima"
e: For Ajneya, external pressure can fill pages, but authentic art requires the inner fire of genuine realization.

q: What truth about the creative process is revealed by "Hiroshima" being written on a train back in India rather than in Japan?
o: Deep realization matures quietly within the mind and bursts into artistic form when the creative moment arrives
The writer forgot Hindi in Japan
Sitting on a train turns anyone into a poet
Poems can only be written inside moving trains
e: Genuine realization incubates quietly in the psyche and surfaces naturally in words when inwardly ripe.

q: Passage: "I write because only by writing can I recognize that inner compulsion." — What self-awareness of the writer does this show?
o: The writer knows nothing at all before writing
Writing is solely for lecturing others
The writer writes merely to improve memory
Writing serves as a tool of self-discovery and a mirror to understand one’s own inner self
e: Ajneya views writing not merely as expression, but as self-inquiry that clarifies the writer’s own inner feelings.

q: By mentioning his science background and knowledge of radioactivity, what limitation does Ajneya highlight?
o: Radioactivity causes no harm
Scientific facts are always false
Intellectual or scientific knowledge stays in the head and cannot replace emotional empathy with human suffering
Science students should never write literature
e: Facts and theory inform the intellect, whereas literature demands that truth touch the heart’s sensibility.

q: Passage: "I write to free myself from inner compulsion and view it objectively (tatastha)." — What does "viewing objectively" mean here?
o: Breaking the pen in anger
Externalizing intense emotion into words so one can contemplate it with calm artistic detachment
Turning away from social issues
Fearing to take any stand
e: Unexpressed turmoil clouds judgment; putting it into words creates healthy artistic distance for clear reflection.

q: To what everyday situation does Ajneya compare the reminders of editors and publishers?
o: An alarm or external prompt nudging an already half-awake sleeper out of bed
Buying vegetables in a market
Crossing a river by boat
Taking a classroom exam
e: The creative seed already exists within; an editor’s nudge simply acts like an alarm clock prompting it into action.

q: What broader human message does the "bright shadow on the scorched stone" convey?
o: Promotion of painting on stones
Support for using scientific weapons in more wars
Praise of Japanese architecture
A profound plea for humanity and compassion against the horror of nuclear weapons and war
e: Ajneya’s realization is a poignant humanist protest against the catastrophic misuse of science in nuclear warfare.

q: If a student asks whether Ajneya could have written "Hiroshima" without visiting Hiroshima, what does the essay suggest?
o: No, because poetry requires visiting Japan
Because trains run only in Japan
Though he knew radioactivity theoretically, the visceral encounter with the stone shadow sparked the decisive inner realization
Yes, he had already written it from newspapers
e: This shows that while theory provides information, vivid personal encounter sparks authentic creative realization.

q: Why did Ajneya consider the question of whether his poem was "good or bad" secondary?
o: Because quality has no value in literature
Because for the creator, truthfulness to felt realization and release from inner compulsion matter most
Because he disrespected readers’ opinions
Because he thought his poem was terrible
e: Before external critical acclaim, authenticity of experience and inner honesty are paramount to the writer.

q: How does the "responsibility of a writer" emerge in "Main Kyon Likhta Hoon?"?

Driving fast and charging extra money
Never speaking to tourists
Exaggerating with false stories
e: Jiten combined communicative warmth, local lore, safe driving on risky roads, and deep empathy for mountain people.

q: Why is the environmental awareness presented in "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi" highly relevant to India today?
o: Because nobody visits mountains anymore
Because no rivers remain in India
Because snow has increased excessively everywhere
Because uncontrolled tourism, litter, and global warming severely threaten Himalayan glaciers and fragile ecosystems
e: Reduced snow in Yumthang and Katao’s unspoiled charm underscore the urgent need for sustainable, eco-friendly tourism.

o: Building roads harms society
Money is unnecessary in hills
Laborers who build society’s essential infrastructure receive meager rewards while everyone else enjoys the fruits of their toil
Workers refuse to work
e: Even amid a travelogue, Madhu Kankaria raises a poignant ethical question about the undervaluation of manual laborers.

q: Describing the Himalayas as "nature’s water pillars" reveals which perspective of the author?
o: Viewing the Himalayas as a commodity
A poetic yet ecological grasp of interdependence—that mountain snow sustains life across the distant plains
Merely a hobby of playing in snow
Opposition to all rivers
e: She recognizes the Himalayas not merely as a tourist backdrop, but as the life-giving watershed of the entire subcontinent.

o: Gratitude toward soldiers, patriotism, and a sense of civic responsibility
Incitement to war
Advice to ban mountain travel
Fear of joining the army
e: She reminds travelers that civilian peace and leisure are safeguarded by the daily sacrifices of soldiers on the frontier.

Integrating peace, reverence for nature, and cleanliness seamlessly into everyday cultural life

Locals dislike their own mountains

o: Authentic writing is born not of fame or external pressure, but of an inner compulsion to recognize and express felt truth
Writing is merely a commercial job

Nobody can write well without visiting Japan
e: Ajneya defines creative writing as an inner journey of sensibility, imagination, realization, and self-discovery above external pressures.

e: When an external sight touches our sensibility deeply enough to transform us within, raw experience becomes realization.

q: What shared creative thread connects Madhu Kankaria in "Sana-Sana Haath Jodi" and Ajneya in "Main Kyon Likhta Hoon?"?
o: Both visited Hiroshima
Both authors hated writing
When an external journey or sight collides with deep inner sensibility, it transforms into meaningful, humane literature
Both wrote only science research papers
e: Madhu Kankaria internalizes Sikkim’s workers and nature empathetically, just as Ajneya turns Hiroshima’s stone shadow into heartfelt poetry.

q: Through the Hiroshima episode, what warning does Ajneya imply about the misuse of science?
o: Writers must never critique science

Nuclear bombs are necessary for peace
e: Knowledge of radioactivity is science, while feeling the agony of a vaporized person’s shadow is conscience—science without conscience destroys.

q: Why is "detachment" (tatasthata) necessary in the writing process according to Ajneya?

So the writer can finish quickly and sleep
e: Overwhelming emotion blurs vision; expressing it onto paper gives the writer the clarity of an objective observer.

q: Does Ajneya treat external factors (editors, publishers, money) as completely nonexistent or irrelevant to writers?

q: Which core idea in Ajneya’s essay best demonstrates his spirit of "self-examination" (aatma-shodh)?
